title: The Pianist
full_review:
Making his first film in his native Poland in 40 years, director Roman Polanski dramatizes the autobiography of a Jewish musician who survived World War II hiding out in empty Warsaw apartments. "The Pianist" (Universal Focus) is surely a very personal work for the filmmaker who himself escaped the Krakow ghetto when he was only 7.

Surprisingly for a Holocaust-themed film by a director with four Oscar nominations to his credit, the movie fails to have the expected emotional impact. In scrupulously avoiding any shred of sentimentality, and depicting the plight of the Jews in very restrained visuals, the dramatic tension doesn't build.

Also, Adrien Brody in the title role as composer and pianist Wladyslaw Szpilman gives an unemotional performance that doesn't begin to convey the pain, fear, starvation and isolation the imperiled musician must have felt separated from his family and his music.

The gradual destruction of a great city, however, is convincingly captured on film and one certainly feels for the innocent populace stripped of their homes, livelihood and finally their precious lives.

It opens in 1939; Szpilman, though only in his late 20s, is already a well-known pianist whose live radio performance is cut short by bombs dropped on Warsaw. He returns home to his well-to-do parents, two sisters and brother; the family feels certain that with England and France entering the war against Germany, all will be well again in a short time.

Instead, to their increasing horror and dismay, they are shuttled into the squalor of the ghetto and reduced to selling the all-important family piano in an excellent scene in which the buyer cruelly exploits their desperation to get money for food. Szpilman assures his close and loving family that this too will pass.

Tragically, they are herded onto a deportation train bound for the camps when a Jewish ghetto cop acquaintance pulls Szpilman alone off. The rest of the movie follows the mortally endangered Jew as a series of people alert him to vacant apartments -- and too infrequently provide him with food. From these various abodes we see the Nazis on the streets killing at will and whole neighborhoods being bombed and reduced to rubble.

Emaciated as the war winds down, Szpilman is discovered by a German officer who decides not to shoot him after making him play on the piano in his hiding spot. The transforming power of art saves his life but in an ironic twist the soldier is not so fortunate.

Polanski captures telling visual details of the occupation and ghetto life as well as instances of inhumanity by Poles, Jews and Germans alike. Yet Brody's aloofness in the role does not serve the story well as there is little sense of urgency to his situation.

In the end, "The Pianist" comes off as a solid film which happily ends on a note of survival and hope, but one whose dispassionate tone may hurt its reception.

Due to intermittent violence and a few instances of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
